{{short description|About algebraic curves passing through all intersection points of two other curves}}
{{More footnotes|date=October 2019}}

In [[algebraic geometry]] the '''AF+BG theorem''' (also known as '''Max Noether's fundamental theorem''') is a result of [[Max Noether]] that asserts that, if  the equation of an [[algebraic curve]] in the [[complex projective plane]] belongs locally (at each intersection point) to the [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] generated by the equations of two other algebraic curves, then it belongs globally to this ideal.

== Statement==
Let {{mvar|F}}, {{mvar|G}}, and {{mvar|H}} be [[homogeneous polynomial]]s in three variables, with {{mvar|H}} having higher degree than {{mvar|F}} and {{mvar|G}}; let {{math|1=''a'' = deg ''H'' − deg ''F''}} and {{math|1=''b'' = deg ''H'' − deg ''G''}} (both positive integers) be the differences of the degrees of the polynomials. Suppose that the [[polynomial greatest common divisor|greatest common divisor]] of {{mvar|F}} and {{mvar|G}} is a constant, which means that the [[projective curve]]s that they define in the projective plane {{tmath|\mathbb P^2}} have an intersection consisting in a finite number of points. For each point {{mvar|P}} of this intersection, the polynomials {{mvar|F}} and {{mvar|G}} generate an [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] {{math|(''F'', ''G'')<sub>''P''</sub>}} of the [[local ring]] of {{tmath|\mathbb P^2}} at {{mvar|P}} (this local ring is the ring of the fractions {{tmath|\tfrac n d,}} where {{mvar|n}} and {{mvar|d}} are polynomials in three variables and {{math|''d''(''P'') ≠ 0}}). The theorem asserts that, if {{mvar|H}} lies in {{math|(''F'', ''G'')<sub>''P''</sub>}} for every intersection point {{mvar|P}}, then {{mvar|H}} lies in the ideal {{math|(''F'', ''G'')}}; that is, there are homogeneous polynomials {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}} of degrees {{mvar|a}} and {{mvar|b}}, respectively, such that {{math|1=''H'' = ''AF'' + ''BG''}}. Furthermore, any two choices of {{mvar|A}} differ by a multiple of {{mvar|G}}, and similarly any two choices of {{mvar|B}} differ by a multiple of {{mvar|F}}.

==Related results==
This theorem may be viewed as a generalization of [[Bézout's identity]], which provides a condition under which an integer or a univariate polynomial {{mvar|h}} may be expressed as an element of the [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] generated by two other integers or univariate polynomials {{mvar|f}} and {{mvar|g}}: such a representation exists exactly when {{mvar|h}} is a multiple of the [[greatest common divisor]] of {{mvar|f}} and {{mvar|g}}. The AF+BG condition expresses, in terms of [[Divisor (algebraic geometry)|divisors]] (sets of points, with multiplicities), a similar condition under which a [[homogeneous polynomial]] {{mvar|H}} in three variables can be written as an element of the ideal generated by two other polynomials {{mvar|F}} and {{mvar|G}}.

This theorem is also a refinement, for this particular case, of [[Hilbert's Nullstellensatz]], which provides a condition expressing that some power of a polynomial {{mvar|h}} (in any number of variables) belongs to the ideal generated by a finite set of polynomials.
